title: Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible subsets, also called the power set, using backtracking.
shortTitle: Generate All Subsets of a Set (Backtracking / Power Set)
keyPoints: The power set of n elements has exactly 2^n subsets, including the empty set and the full set
Backtracking explores include-or-exclude for each element via the add-recurse-remove rhythm
Record the current path at every recursive call, not just at leaves, because every prefix is a valid subset
Always store a copy of the path when recording, because the path is mutated throughout the search
Starting the loop at the current index prevents generating the same subset in different orders
Alternative approaches include iterative cascade and bitmask enumeration
Time complexity is O(n * 2^n) because each of 2^n subsets is copied in O(n)

s1_definition.oneliner: For each element choose include or exclude; every complete choice sequence is one subset, giving 2^n subsets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Power set** – the collection of all subsets of a set, including the empty set and the full set.
- **Count** – a set of n elements has exactly 2^n subsets.
- **Backtracking** – walk elements in order; at each element, branch into include and exclude. Each path from start to end is one subset.
- **Recording** – record the path at every call (not just leaves), because every prefix of choices is a valid subset.
- **Copy rule** – always store `new ArrayList<>(path)` when recording, since the path mutates.
- **Complexity** – O(n * 2^n) time and O(n * 2^n) space for the output.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services on an account, and Priya wants to see every possible combination, from choosing nothing to choosing everything. A clerk goes through the add-ons one at a time, and for each one she branches into two worlds: one where the customer takes it and one where she skips it. Every distinct sequence of take-or-skip choices is one possible service package.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Subset Generation: Backtracking for [1, 2, 3]

  backtrack(start=0, path=[])
  ├── record []
  ├── i=0: path=[1]
  │   ├── record [1]
  │   ├── i=1: path=[1,2]
  │   │   ├── record [1,2]
  │   │   └── i=2: path=[1,2,3]
  │   │       └── record [1,2,3]
  │   └── i=2: path=[1,3]
  │       └── record [1,3]
  ├── i=1: path=[2]
  │   ├── record [2]
  │   └── i=2: path=[2,3]
  │       └── record [2,3]
  └── i=2: path=[3]
      └── record [3]

  Total: 8 subsets = 2^3
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The power set is the collection of all subsets of a set, and a set of n elements has exactly 2^n subsets including the empty set. Backtracking generates them by walking elements in order and branching into include or exclude at each element. The add-recurse-remove rhythm at each step is the essence of backtracking.

The key detail is that you record the path at every recursive call, not just at leaves, because every prefix of choices is a valid subset. The empty path at the first call captures the empty subset. Always store a copy of the path when recording, because the path is mutated throughout the search.

Starting the loop at the current index prevents generating the same subset in different orders. For inputs with duplicates, sort first and skip consecutive equal values at the same recursion level. The bitmask alternative is extremely compact but backtracking generalizes best to constrained variants.

At the National Bank of India, the marketing team used this to enumerate every possible combination of optional account services for pricing and bundling. The start-index discipline guaranteed each package appeared exactly once.

Remember one sentence: record at every call, copy the path, start at the current index, and you get all 2^n subsets.
